Moles and Mass.intro: The mole is the unit used to count atoms and molecules. Understanding moles allows chemists to calculate the amounts of substances in reactions.
Moles and Mass.mnemonic: Use the 'Mole Triangle' — draw a triangle with Mass on top, and Moles × Mr at the bottom. Cover what you want to find: Mass = Moles × Mr; Moles = Mass ÷ Mr; Mr = Mass ÷ Moles. Or remember: 'Mr Mole has Mass!' (Mr × Moles = Mass).

sections.title: The Mole
sections.text: The mole is the chemist's counting unit. One mole of any substance contains 6.02 × 10²³ particles and has a mass equal to its relative formula mass in grams.
points: 1 mole = 6.02 × 10²³ particles — this is Avogadro's number (NA)
Molar mass — the mass of 1 mole of a substance in grams = its relative formula mass (Mr) in g/mol
Formula: moles = mass ÷ Mr — the most important formula in quantitative chemistry
Rearranged: mass = moles × Mr; Mr = mass ÷ moles
Worked example 1 — moles of 18 g of H₂O (Mr = 18): moles = 18 ÷ 18 = 1 mol
Worked example 2 — mass of 2 mol of CaCO₃ (Mr = 100): mass = 2 × 100 = 200 g

callout.label: Triangle Formula
callout.text: Moles = Mass ÷ Mr | Mass = Moles × Mr | Mr = Mass ÷ Moles

sections.title: Relative Formula Mass (Mr)
sections.text: The relative formula mass (Mr) of a compound is the sum of all relative atomic masses in its formula. It is used in all mole calculations.
points: Add up all relative atomic masses — use the periodic table for Ar values
Example: H₂O — (2 × 1) + 16 = 18
Example: CaCO₃ — 40 + 12 + (3 × 16) = 40 + 12 + 48 = 100
Example: H₂SO₄ — (2 × 1) + 32 + (4 × 16) = 2 + 32 + 64 = 98
Multiply by subscripts — e.g. in Ca(OH)₂: Ca + 2×(O + H) = 40 + 2×(16+1) = 40 + 34 = 74
Mr has no units — it is a ratio (relative to carbon-12)

sections.title: Using Moles in Reacting Mass Calculations
sections.text: Molar ratios from balanced equations allow us to calculate the masses of reactants and products.
points: Step 1 — write and balance the equation
Step 2 — calculate moles of the given substance (moles = mass ÷ Mr)
Step 3 — use the molar ratio from the equation to find moles of the desired substance
Step 4 — convert moles back to mass (mass = moles × Mr)
Worked example — 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO: how much MgO from 24 g Mg (Mr = 24)? Moles Mg = 24÷24 = 1 mol; ratio 2:2 so 1 mol MgO formed; mass MgO = 1 × 40 = 40 g
Ratio matters — always read the coefficients in the balanced equation as the mole ratio

keyTerms.def: The amount of substance containing 6.02 × 10²³ particles (Avogadro's number)
The sum of all relative atomic masses in a chemical formula
The mass of one mole of a substance in grams — numerically equal to Mr
6.02 × 10²³ — the number of particles in one mole of any substance
The ratio of moles of reactants and products given by coefficients in a balanced equation
The weighted average mass of an atom of an element relative to carbon-12

examTips: Show working clearly in all mole calculations — write the formula, substitute values, then calculate.
moles = mass ÷ Mr is the key formula; always identify which substance you're calculating moles for first.
Always check units: mass in grams, volume in dm³ — never mix units mid-calculation.
Multiply by subscripts when calculating Mr — e.g. for SO₄²⁻: 32 + (4 × 16) = 96.
commonMistakes: Using mass number from the periodic table instead of relative atomic mass — for GCSE these are often the same, but use the Ar value.
Forgetting to multiply by subscripts in formulas — e.g. O₃ = 3 × 16 = 48, not 16.
Not reading the molar ratio from the balanced equation — a 2:1 ratio means you must halve or double the moles.
clozePassages: The mole is the unit used by chemists to measure amounts of substance. One mole contains 6.02 × 10²³ particles — this is called Avogadro's number. The molar mass of a substance is its relative formula mass in grams. For example, one mole of water (H₂O) has a molar mass of 18 g/mol. The formula to calculate moles is: moles = mass ÷ molar mass.

The relative formula mass (Mr) of a compound is calculated by adding up the relative atomic masses of all the atoms in its formula. For example, NaCl has an Mr of 23 + 35.5 = 58.5. Using moles allows chemists to calculate the exact masses of reactants and products in a chemical reaction. Reacting masses can be calculated by using the molar ratio from the balanced equation.

Chemists use the concept of the mole to work out how much of each reactant is needed and how much product is made. The balanced equation gives the ratio of moles of reactants to products. For example, if 2 moles of hydrogen react with 1 mole of oxygen, 2 moles of water are produced. Using this ratio and molar masses, the masses of reactants and products in any reaction can be calculated.

Conservation of Mass.intro: In chemical reactions, mass is always conserved — atoms are rearranged but not created or destroyed.
Conservation of Mass.mnemonic: Remember: 'Atoms are like Lego bricks — you rearrange them but never lose them.' Mass in = Mass out. If mass seems to change, think: is a GAS escaping (mass decreases) or is a gas being ABSORBED from the air (mass increases)?

sections.title: The Law of Conservation of Mass
sections.text: In any chemical reaction, the total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products. No atoms are created or destroyed.
points: Total mass of reactants = total mass of products — always, in any reaction
Atoms are rearranged — bonds are broken and new ones form, but atoms are not created or destroyed
Balanced equations reflect this — same number of each type of atom on both sides
Apparent mass decrease — a gas has been produced and escaped (e.g. CO₂ from CaCO₃ decomposition)
Apparent mass increase — a gas has been absorbed from the air (e.g. magnesium burning in oxygen — Mg + O₂ → MgO)
Closed vs open systems — in a closed system, mass is always constant; in an open system, gases can escape

sections.title: Balancing Equations
sections.text: Balanced equations ensure the same number of atoms appear on each side, reflecting conservation of mass.
points: Add coefficients (big numbers) in front of formulas — never change subscripts within a formula
Check each element — count atoms on each side; adjust coefficients until equal
Example — H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl: 2 H and 2 Cl each side; balanced
Example — CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O: C:1=1, H:4=4, O:4=4; balanced
Ionic equations — can also be balanced; charge must balance as well as atoms
State symbols — (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) aqueous (dissolved)

callout.label: Example
callout.text: H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl (balanced: 2 H atoms and 2 Cl atoms on each side)

sections.title: Reacting Mass Calculations using Conservation of Mass
sections.text: Conservation of mass allows us to find missing masses in reactions without needing to know the full equation.
points: Find missing mass — if all other masses are known: missing mass = total reactant mass − known product masses
Worked example — 10 g CaCO₃ heated; 5.6 g CaO remains. Mass of CO₂ = 10 − 5.6 = 4.4 g
Verify with formula masses — CaCO₃ (Mr = 100), CaO (Mr = 56), CO₂ (Mr = 44): ratio 100:56:44 matches
Percentage composition — % by mass of element = (Ar × number of atoms ÷ Mr) × 100
Example % composition — % Fe in Fe₂O₃: Mr = 160; % Fe = (2×56 ÷ 160) × 100 = 70%

keyTerms.def: The total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products in any chemical reaction
A chemical equation with equal numbers of each type of atom on both sides
A number placed in front of a formula in an equation to balance it without changing the substance
Symbol showing physical state: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) aqueous
A system where no matter can enter or leave — total mass is always constant
The percentage by mass of each element in a compound

examTips: If a reaction in an open container appears to lose mass, always state: 'a gas was produced and escaped into the atmosphere'.
Always check balanced equations before using them in calculations — AQA may give unbalanced equations to test this.
When finding a missing mass, simply subtract known product masses from total reactant mass — show this clearly in your working.
commonMistakes: Forgetting that in an open container, gas can escape — causing an apparent mass decrease, not a violation of conservation of mass.
Changing subscripts to balance equations instead of adding coefficients — NEVER change subscripts (e.g. H₂O must stay H₂O, not H₃O).
Not accounting for all products — remember reactions can produce gases like CO₂ or H₂O vapour that aren't always obvious.
clozePassages: The law of conservation of mass states that mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. The total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products. This is because atoms are rearranged but not created or destroyed. Chemical equations must be balanced — the number of each type of atom must be the same on both sides of the equation.

When a reaction appears to show a change in mass, it can usually be explained. If a solid seems to gain mass, it may be reacting with oxygen from the air. If mass appears to be lost, it may be because a gas has been produced and escaped. For example, when calcium carbonate is heated, carbon dioxide gas is released, so the solid remaining has less mass. In a closed system, total mass always remains constant.

Balancing equations reflects the law of conservation of mass. In a balanced equation, the number of atoms of each element is equal on both sides. Coefficients are placed in front of formulae to balance the equation — never subscripts within the formula. For example, the equation for burning hydrogen: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O shows that 2 moles of hydrogen react with 1 mole of oxygen to produce 2 moles of water.

Yield and Atom Economy.intro: In real reactions, the actual yield is often less than the theoretical maximum. Atom economy measures how efficiently reactant atoms end up in useful products.
Yield and Atom Economy.mnemonic: For % yield: 'What you GOT over what you were SUPPOSED to get, × 100' — GOT ÷ SUPPOSED × 100. For atom economy: 'Useful Mr over All Mr × 100' — think of a factory: atom economy = useful output ÷ total output × 100. High both = green chemistry!

sections.title: Percentage Yield
sections.text: Percentage yield compares how much product was actually made to the theoretical maximum. It is always 100% or less.
points: Formula — % yield = (actual yield ÷ theoretical yield) × 100
Theoretical yield — maximum mass of product possible, calculated from moles
Actual yield — mass of product actually obtained in the experiment
Reasons yield < 100% — reversible reaction doesn't go to completion; product lost in filtration/evaporation; side reactions occur; incomplete reaction
Worked example — theoretical yield = 50 g; actual yield = 35 g: % yield = (35 ÷ 50) × 100 = 70%
Industrial importance — higher yield = less waste, lower cost, more profitable

sections.title: Atom Economy
sections.text: Atom economy measures what percentage of the total mass of reactant atoms ends up in the desired product. High atom economy = less waste.
points: Formula — % atom economy = (Mr of desired product ÷ sum of Mr of all products) × 100
High atom economy — more atoms end up in useful product; less waste; more sustainable
Addition reactions = 100% atom economy — all atoms from reactants go into the single product
Substitution reactions — have lower atom economy because by-products are also formed
Worked example — CH₂=CH₂ + H₂ → CH₃CH₃ (addition): all atoms in product = 100% atom economy
Worked example 2 — CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂: desired product CaO (Mr = 56); all products 56+44 = 100: atom economy = (56÷100)×100 = 56%

callout.label: Formula
callout.text: % atom economy = (Mr of desired product ÷ sum of Mr of all products) × 100

sections.title: Green Chemistry and Sustainability
sections.text: Both percentage yield and atom economy are important in making industrial chemistry more sustainable and economically viable.
points: Green chemistry — aims for high yield AND high atom economy to reduce waste and energy use
High yield — means less raw material is wasted; more economical
High atom economy — fewer by-products to dispose of; reduces pollution; more sustainable
Catalysts improve both — increase rate and yield without appearing in the products; not consumed
Industrial trade-off — the most atom-economical reaction may not always be the fastest or cheapest

keyTerms.def: The actual yield as a percentage of the maximum theoretical yield: (actual ÷ theoretical) × 100
The proportion of reactant atoms that end up in the desired product: (Mr of desired product ÷ total Mr of all products) × 100
The maximum possible mass of product calculated from the moles and balanced equation
The mass of product actually obtained in a real experiment
The design of reactions and processes to reduce waste and environmental impact
A reaction where all atoms from the reactants combine into one product — gives 100% atom economy

examTips: % yield asks: how much did we get vs how much we expected? Atom economy asks: of all the atoms used, how many ended up in useful product? — distinguish these clearly.
Addition reactions always have 100% atom economy — state this and the reason (only one product formed).
Show all working for % yield calculations: write formula, substitute actual and theoretical values, calculate.
commonMistakes: Confusing % yield (comparing actual to expected amount) with atom economy (how efficiently atoms are used) — they measure different things.
Calculating atom economy using masses of reactants instead of masses of products — use the Mr of products, not reactants.
Saying % yield can be greater than 100% — it cannot; actual yield cannot exceed theoretical yield.
clozePassages: The percentage yield of a reaction compares the actual amount of product obtained to the maximum theoretical yield. It is calculated as: (actual yield ÷ theoretical yield) × 100. Yields are rarely 100% because reactions may be reversible, some product may be lost during separation, or side reactions may occur. Maximising yield is important in industrial chemistry to reduce waste and increase profitability.

Atom economy measures how much of the starting materials end up as useful product. The formula is: (molar mass of desired product ÷ total molar mass of all products) × 100. A high atom economy means less waste is produced. Addition reactions have 100% atom economy because only one product is formed. Substitution reactions have lower atom economy as other products are also formed. High atom economy is important for sustainable chemistry.

In industrial chemistry, both percentage yield and atom economy are important. A high atom economy means the reaction produces fewer unwanted by-products, reducing waste and the cost of disposal. Industrial chemists try to find reaction conditions and catalysts that maximise yield and atom economy. The principles of green chemistry aim to design processes that are more efficient, less wasteful, and less harmful to the environment.

Concentration.intro: Concentration measures how much solute is dissolved in a given volume of solution. It is essential for quantitative chemistry calculations.
Concentration.mnemonic: Use the 'CVn triangle' — Concentration (mol/dm³), Volume (dm³), moles (n) — just like the moles triangle. Cover the variable you want: C = n ÷ V; n = C × V; V = n ÷ C. Always convert cm³ to dm³ by dividing by 1000 BEFORE using the formula!

sections.title: Concentration Formula
sections.text: Concentration tells us how many moles of solute are in each dm³ of solution. The higher the concentration, the more solute particles per unit volume.
points: Formula — concentration (mol/dm³) = moles ÷ volume (dm³)
Also — concentration (g/dm³) = mass (g) ÷ volume (dm³)
Units — mol/dm³ (most common); g/dm³; M (molar — same as mol/dm³)
Worked example 1 — 0.5 mol NaCl dissolved in 2 dm³: concentration = 0.5 ÷ 2 = 0.25 mol/dm³
Worked example 2 — 2 mol/dm³ HCl, 250 cm³ (= 0.25 dm³): moles = 2 × 0.25 = 0.5 mol
Effect on rate — more concentrated solution → more solute particles per dm³ → more frequent collisions → faster reaction

callout.label: Formula
callout.text: Concentration (mol/dm³) = moles ÷ volume (dm³). Also: concentration (g/dm³) = mass ÷ volume

sections.title: Converting Units
sections.text: Volume unit conversion is a common source of errors. Always convert cm³ to dm³ before using in the concentration formula.
points: 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³ = 1 litre
cm³ → dm³: divide by 1000 — e.g. 250 cm³ = 0.25 dm³
dm³ → cm³: multiply by 1000 — e.g. 0.1 dm³ = 100 cm³
More concentrated — more solute particles dissolved in the same volume of solution

sections.title: Titration and Calculating Concentrations
sections.text: Titration is a practical technique used to find the concentration of an unknown solution using a solution of known concentration.
points: Titration — add solution from a burette to a known volume of another solution until the endpoint (indicator changes colour)
Using titration data — moles of known solution = concentration × volume (in dm³); use molar ratio from equation; find moles of unknown; concentration = moles ÷ volume
Worked example — 25 cm³ NaOH neutralised by 20 cm³ of 0.1 mol/dm³ HCl: moles HCl = 0.1 × 0.020 = 0.002 mol; ratio 1:1 so moles NaOH = 0.002 mol; concentration NaOH = 0.002 ÷ 0.025 = 0.08 mol/dm³
Repeat titrations — perform concordant titrations (within 0.10 cm³) and average for accuracy
Indicator choice — methyl orange for strong acid/strong base; phenolphthalein also used

keyTerms.def: The amount of solute dissolved per unit volume of solution, measured in mol/dm³ or g/dm³
The substance that is dissolved in a solvent to form a solution
The liquid in which a solute dissolves (often water in chemistry)
Cubic decimetre — a unit of volume equal to 1000 cm³ (1 litre)
A technique to find the concentration of a solution by reacting it with a known volume and concentration of another solution
Titration readings within 0.10 cm³ of each other — used to calculate a reliable average

examTips: ALWAYS convert cm³ to dm³ (÷1000) before using in the concentration formula — this is the most common error in titration calculations.
For titration calculations, always show the 4 steps: moles of known → ratio → moles of unknown → concentration.
Concentration in mol/dm³ is most common in AQA papers; g/dm³ may also appear — check which unit is asked for.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to convert cm³ to dm³ before calculating concentration — dividing by 1000 is essential.
Using the wrong molar ratio in titration calculations — always write and balance the equation first.
Quoting titration averages using anomalous results — only average concordant titres (within 0.10 cm³).
clozePassages: The concentration of a solution is the amount of solute dissolved in a given volume of solvent. It is measured in mol/dm³ (moles per cubic decimetre) or g/dm³ (grams per cubic decimetre). The formula is: concentration = moles ÷ volume. A higher concentration means more solute particles per unit volume, which increases the rate of reaction by increasing the frequency of collisions.

Titration is a technique used to find the concentration of an unknown solution. A known volume of one solution is placed in a conical flask with an indicator. The other solution is added from a burette until the end point is reached — shown by a colour change in the indicator. The volume of solution used (the titre) allows the concentration to be calculated. Titration is used in quality control and research.

When solutions are diluted, the number of moles of solute stays the same but the volume increases, reducing the concentration. The formula C₁V₁ = C₂V₂ can be used to calculate concentrations after dilution. When comparing reactions in solution, concentration determines how frequently particles collide. A more concentrated solution contains more solute particles per dm³, leading to more frequent collisions and a faster reaction rate.

Gas Volumes.intro: Gases are measured by volume rather than mass. At the same temperature and pressure, equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of molecules.
Gas Volumes.mnemonic: Remember: 'At RTP, 1 mole = 24 dm³' — the magic number is 24. To find volume: Moles × 24 = Volume (dm³). To find moles from volume: Volume ÷ 24. Or use the rhyme: '24 dm³ per mole at RTP — that's the rule for you and me!'

sections.title: Molar Volume of Gas
sections.text: At room temperature and pressure, one mole of any gas always occupies 24 dm³ (24,000 cm³), regardless of the type of gas.
points: At RTP: 1 mole of any gas = 24 dm³ — applies to all gases (H₂, O₂, CO₂, N₂ etc.)
Volume of gas — volume (dm³) = moles × 24
Moles of gas from volume — moles = volume (dm³) ÷ 24
Worked example 1 — volume of 0.5 mol CO₂ at RTP: volume = 0.5 × 24 = 12 dm³
Worked example 2 — moles of gas in 6 dm³ at RTP: moles = 6 ÷ 24 = 0.25 mol
Converting units — 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³; at RTP, 1 mole = 24,000 cm³

callout.label: Key Fact
callout.text: At room temperature and pressure (RTP): 1 mole of any gas occupies 24 dm³ (24,000 cm³).

sections.title: Using Gas Volumes in Calculations
sections.text: Gas volume ratios match the molar ratios in balanced equations. This allows direct comparison of gas volumes without calculating mass.
points: Volume ratio = mole ratio — at the same temperature and pressure, volume is proportional to moles
Example — H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl: 1 volume H₂ + 1 volume Cl₂ → 2 volumes HCl
Example 2 — 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O: 2 volumes H₂ react with 1 volume O₂
Worked example — 48 dm³ H₂ reacts with O₂ (ratio 2:1): volume O₂ needed = 48 ÷ 2 = 24 dm³
Mixed calculations — can combine moles, mass, concentration, and gas volume in multi-step problems

sections.title: Factors Affecting Gas Volume
sections.text: Temperature and pressure affect the volume of a gas. At constant temperature, increasing pressure decreases volume; at constant pressure, increasing temperature increases volume.
points: Temperature effect — higher temperature → particles move faster → gas expands (greater volume)
Pressure effect — higher pressure → particles pushed closer together → smaller volume
RTP = room temperature and pressure — defined as 25°C (298 K) and 1 atmosphere (101 kPa)
STP (standard) — sometimes used: 0°C and 1 atm; molar volume at STP = 22.4 dm³
Industrial relevance — industrial reactors must account for T and P effects on gas volumes

keyTerms.def: The volume occupied by one mole of gas — at RTP this is 24 dm³ for any gas
Room temperature and pressure — defined as 25°C and 1 atmosphere; used for gas volume calculations
Cubic decimetre — a unit of volume equal to 1 litre = 1000 cm³
Equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules
The ratio of volumes of gases in a reaction — equal to the mole ratio from the balanced equation

examTips: At RTP: 1 mole of ANY gas = 24 dm³ — memorise this and use it for all gas volume calculations.
Gas volume ratio = mole ratio from the balanced equation — use this for comparing volumes of different gases.
Always check if the volume is in dm³ or cm³ — convert cm³ to dm³ (÷1000) before using the 24 dm³/mol formula.
commonMistakes: Confusing dm³ and cm³ — 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³; 1 mole at RTP = 24 dm³ = 24,000 cm³.
Using 22.4 dm³ instead of 24 dm³ — 22.4 is at STP (0°C); at RTP (25°C) use 24 dm³.
Forgetting that gas volume ratio equals mole ratio — 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O means 2 volumes H₂ react with 1 volume O₂.
clozePassages: At the same temperature and pressure, equal volumes of all gases contain the same number of moles. At room temperature and pressure (RTP), one mole of any gas occupies 24 dm³ (24,000 cm³). This allows the volume of a gas to be calculated from the number of moles using: volume = moles × molar volume (24 dm³). This is useful for calculating volumes of gases produced or used in reactions.

The volume of a gas is affected by temperature and pressure. Increasing temperature increases the volume of a gas (at constant pressure) because the particles move faster and spread out more. Increasing pressure decreases the volume (at constant temperature) by pushing particles closer together. These relationships are described by Boyle's Law and Charles's Law. Industrial processes must account for these factors when working with gases.

Gases in a mixture each exert their own partial pressure. The total pressure of a gas mixture equals the sum of the partial pressures of each gas. When calculating reacting volumes of gases, the molar ratios from the balanced equation can be used directly, since equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of moles. This simplifies calculations involving gaseous reactions.
